claims.text: Engineered segregation of selected solutes to grain boundaries reduces high-temperature grain-boundary sliding.
Engineered grain-boundary solute segregation modifies dislocation-climb behavior.
Grain-boundary sliding and dislocation climb govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in the proposed fusion structural materials.
As-fabricated tungsten alloys or reduced-activation steels possess native grain-boundary chemistry, dislocation networks, and precipitate distributions.
Targeted alloying or heat treatment can be used to induce controlled solute segregation and modify grain-boundary chemistry.
Temperatures of approximately 800–1000 K are representative of high-temperature fusion-reactor conditions for these components.
Modified grain-boundary chemistry alters interfacial cohesion.
Modified grain-boundary chemistry alters interfacial diffusion kinetics.
At elevated temperature, dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding dominate deformation.
Segregated solutes lower grain-boundary energy.
Lower grain-boundary energy caused by segregated solutes increases resistance to grain-boundary sliding.
Increased sliding resistance delays grain-boundary weakening and reduces localized plastic deformation.
Mitigating strain localization and grain-boundary crack initiation improves toughness.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, solute-segregated material will have a lower high-temperature plastic-strain rate because its grain-boundary sliding rate is lower.
Relative to the baseline, solute-segregated material will exhibit improved toughness and increased strain to failure.
Solute-segregated material will exhibit altered dislocation-density distributions and delayed dislocation accumulation at grain boundaries.
The hypothesis is limited to approximately 800–1000 K, where thermally activated climb and grain-boundary sliding contribute significantly to deformation.
The hypothesis is not expected to apply after extensive dynamic recrystallization or phase transformation.
The magnitudes of the changes in plastic-strain rate and toughness may depend on solute identity, alloy system, and processing conditions.

Failure to produce statistically significant changes in grain-boundary sliding or dislocation climb together with no toughness improvement relative to the same-alloy baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
